https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/worl.text: In the middle of the Netherlands, an unusual experiment in conservation began with an unlikely raw material: mud. Instead of treating the vast quantities of sediment accumulating on the floor of Markermeer as waste, Dutch engineers used it to create a new landscape. They built a chain of islands from sand, clay, silt and other material dredged from the lake, creating beaches, shallow waters, marshes and sheltered habitats where very little suitable habitat had existed before.The project, called Marker Wadden, was designed to help revive the ecology of Markermeer, a large freshwater lake whose ecosystem had deteriorated after decades of human intervention. But the most remarkable part came afterwards. Nature began moving in.Within just a few years, the newly created islands were being colonised by plants, insects and fish, while thousands of migratory and breeding birds began using the area for feeding, nesting and resting. What started as a huge engineering project was gradually becoming a living ecosystem. The project also demonstrated how carefully designed artificial landscapes can recreate the varied shallow-water and wetland conditions that many native species need, turning a degraded lake into a more diverse and functional habitat.Why the Netherlands needed to build new islandsMarkermeer is a man-made freshwater lake created through one of the Netherlands' enormous water-management projects. Before the lake was separated from the sea, the area was part of the Zuiderzee, a saltwater inlet of the North Sea. The construction of the Afsluitdijk in 1932 cut the Zuiderzee off from the North Sea, turning it into the freshwater IJsselmeer. Further engineering works eventually created Markermeer as a separate lake.These interventions transformed the landscape but also created an ecological problem. Markermeer is shallow and exposed, and large quantities of fine sediment can be stirred up from its bottom. The resulting cloudy water makes it difficult for sunlight to penetrate, affecting aquatic plants and the organisms that depend on them.The lake also lacked many of the shallow, sheltered habitats that support young fish, aquatic plants and waterbirds. Conservationists therefore proposed a radical solution: rather than trying to remove the sediment, use it to build new habitat. The concept became Marker Wadden. Instead of treating the sediment solely as waste, engineers began seeing it as a valuable raw material for rebuilding habitats the lake had lost.Millions of tonnes of sediment became a new landscapeThe first stage of Marker Wadden was not about creating a conventional island for people. Instead, engineers designed a landscape specifically for wildlife.Material from the bottom of Markermeer was dredged and deposited within carefully constructed boundaries. Sand was used to form protective structures, while softer sediment was placed inside them. As the material settled, it formed land at different elevations.This created a mixture of habitats rather than a single flat island. There were sandy beaches, shallow lagoons, wetlands, mudflats and higher areas where vegetation could establish itself. Channels and openings allowed water to move through parts of the landscape, helping create the dynamic conditions found in natural wetlands.According to an article titled âRewilding the planet: An archipelago constructed of sand and mud is bringing new life to a dead lake but can this bold experiment have a lasting impact?â published in Nature, around 37.2 million tonnes of material were dredged during construction, almost all of it from the lake itself. The first island was completed in 2016, with the wider archipelago developed in subsequent stages.The approach was significant because it combined large-scale Dutch engineering with a philosophy sometimes described as building with nature.The engineers created the initial conditions. They did not attempt to control every subsequent change. Wind, waves, sediment, plants and animals would help determine what the islands eventually became.Birds were among the first visitors of the islandThe speed at which wildlife began using Marker Wadden surprised even some of the people involved. The barren-looking islands soon attracted birds, including species that needed somewhere to rest or breed away from the exposed waters of Markermeer.As reported by the Department of Avian Ecology and Migration, Museum and Institute of Zoology, Polish Academy of Sciences, pioneer birds such as terns began arriving while parts of the landscape were still being formed. Some birds even travelled to the North Sea to find food before returning to the islands.As vegetation and aquatic life developed, the number and variety of birds increased. By 2021, 47 bird species were breeding on Marker Wadden. Around 60,000 migratory birds used the islands during the year to July 2021, according to the Nature report.Among the visitors were Eurasian spoonbills, greater flamingos and gull-billed terns. The appearance of gull-billed terns was particularly notable because the species had not bred in the Netherlands for decades.The islands were therefore becoming more than isolated pieces of land. They were turning into an important stopover and breeding area within a wider network of European wetlands.The transformation was happening underwater tooThe birds provided the most visible evidence of change, but much of Marker Wadden's ecological development was taking place beneath the water.The new sheltered areas created conditions for aquatic plants and small organisms to establish themselves. Fish began using the shallow waters, particularly as nursery habitat for younger individuals.Researchers recorded numerous fish species around the islands, alongside fish larvae and a range of smaller organisms forming the foundations of the developing food web.This is important because the original problem in Markermeer was not simply that there were too few islands. The lake had lost a variety of habitats.By introducing shallow, sheltered areas, Marker Wadden created places where organisms at different levels of the food chain could live. Plants and microscopic organisms supported insects and small aquatic animals, which in turn provided food for fish and birds.The result was an ecosystem gradually building itself around a landscape that had not existed only a few years earlier.The islands are artificial, but the ecosystem is notThere is an important distinction between building an island and building an ecosystem. The first was done by people. The second is being shaped by nature.The Dutch project did not attempt to recreate an exact historical landscape. Instead, it introduced habitats that were missing from the modern lake and allowed wildlife to determine what would happen next.That makes Marker Wadden an unusual form of ecological restoration. It is not a return to a pristine landscape that existed before human intervention. It is an attempt to create new ecological possibilities within a landscape that has already been heavily engineered.This distinction is central to the reporting in Nature, which presents Marker Wadden as a large-scale experiment in how humans can alter physical conditions and then allow natural processes to take over.The new islands face a natural problemMarker Wadden's success does not mean the islands will remain unchanged. They were built largely from soft sediment, which naturally settles and compacts over time. As water drains from the material and the weight of the islands compresses the layers below, parts of the landscape can gradually sink.For an artificial island, this creates a long-term challenge. Unlike a natural coastal system, Marker Wadden does not receive a regular supply of sediment from tides and rivers that can continually rebuild the land. Researchers therefore continue to monitor how the islands evolve, including changes in their elevation, sediment movement and vegetation.This gradual transformation is not necessarily a failure. The project was designed to allow natural processes to shape the landscape rather than preserve it in exactly the form in which engineers created it. The question is whether those processes can maintain the shallow waters, wetlands and open areas that made the islands valuable to wildlife in the first place.Creating habitat is only the first stepThe changing landscape also raises a wider question for artificial-island projects: how long can newly created habitats continue to support the species they were designed to attract?The aforementioned 2026 study published in Estuaries and Coasts by Dominik Marchowski and colleagues offers an important insight. Researchers examined two artificial islands made from dredged sediment in Poland's Szczecin Lagoon and found that waterbirds colonised them rapidly. The islands soon became important breeding grounds, including for species of conservation concern.But the researchers also found that these benefits can change as vegetation takes hold. On one of the islands, tall vegetation, including reeds and willow, covered less than 1% of the area in 2021 but had expanded to 23% by 2025. Their modelling suggested that continued vegetation growth could substantially reduce the open habitat used by ground-nesting birds within a few years.The finding adds an important qualification to the success story of projects such as Marker Wadden. Building new habitat can give wildlife an immediate boost, but maintaining that habitat may require long-term management. An island that begins as open sand and mud can eventually become a densely vegetated landscape, supporting a very different community of species.Marchowski and his colleagues therefore highlight both the potential and the limitations of dredged-sediment islands. Their isolation can provide valuable breeding refuges with reduced access for terrestrial predators, but the conservation benefits may diminish if the physical and ecological conditions that attracted birds in the first place disappear.Marker Wadden shows how sediment once regarded as a waste material can become a functioning wildlife habitat. The newer research adds another dimension to that story: successful restoration is not only about giving nature somewhere to begin; it is also about understanding how that habitat will change over time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Photograph: Marni Cordell/The Guardian Australia weather Australian ski resorts to close up to a month early due to global heating and El Niño ‘Challenging’ weather conditions and lack of snowfall are being blamed after a winter that broke multiple heat records Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent Fri 4 Sep 2026 02.24 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 02.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Major Australian alpine resorts are closing their ski operations up to a month early after a winter that broke multiple records for heat with limited snow falls being washed away by rain. Predictions in June that a building El Niño could combine with global heating for a challenging ski season came to pass , with seven resorts either already closed or announcing ski lifts will stop operating this weekend. This week the Victorian resorts of Mount Buller, Mount Hotham and Falls Creek, together with Charlotte Pass in New South Wales, all announced ski operations would end this weekend. The Victorian resort of Mount Baw Baw, the NSW resort at Selwyn and Tasmania’s Ben Lomond have already closed. Resorts typically aim to stay open until the first weekend of October. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter Resorts blamed “challenging” weather conditions and lack of snowfall. Two other major NSW resorts at Perisher and Thredbo remain open. “The season was frankly a shocker. This was the fourth disappointing season since 2020,” said Dr Andrew Watkins, a climate scientist and adjunct professor at the Monash University and a science adviser to the campaign group Protect our Winters. “The problems were El Niño and climate change. It was not that dry this year, but the problem was the warmth. The heat just did us in.” Watkins, who is also a keen skier, said winter temperatures had been too high and precipitation that might have fallen as snow, had instead fallen as rain. “Rain is the natural enemy of a snowpack. It melts it and then washes it away,” he said. 0:40 Footage shows first snow of the year falling at Perisher ski resort in New South Wales – video Data from the Bureau of Meteorology show Falls Creek and Mount Hotham had their wettest winters in more than 30 years but, together with Mount Buller, they also had their warmest winters on record for average maximum and minimum temperatures. Watkins said data from weather observations at Cabramurra in Kosciuszko national park suggested alpine winters had warmed by about 2C since the 1960s. He said that temperature rise would have been the difference between precipitation falling as rain instead of snow. “It would have been a bumper season if it had been 50 years ago,” he said. The El Niño currently in place in the Pacific Ocean can promote hotter and drier temperatures in Australia’s south-east in winter and spring. This week the bureau forecast the current El Niño would be the strongest on record and Australian scientists said climate change had made the strength of the event six times more likely. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When he publishes Sign up to Clear Air Australia Adam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisis after newsletter promotion BoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influence Read more A bureau spokesperson said this winter’s heat was consistent “with a developing strong El Niño” and the season had seen long periods of high pressure in the Tasman Sea that directed warmer air from the north over alpine regions. “But winter 2026 also experienced relatively warm nights, with cloud cover and moist soils resulting in less overnight cooling,” the spokesperson said. “This is in contrast with historical El Niño events. This is all occurring against the background of a globally warmer climate, with daily global surface air temperatures since June close to or above the record levels in 2024.” New South Wales, Tasmania and Victoria all recorded their hottest winters on record this year. In July, many ski resorts broke all-time heat records for the month with temperatures during one hot spell up to 12C above average . Climate scientists have been warning for decades that global heating will create a challenging future for Australia’s ski resorts and alpine habitats. Josh Elliott, chief executive at the representative body Snow Resorts Australia, said there was “no question it has been a challenging season for natural snowfall”. “This winter was shaped by a combination of abnormally warm weather and climatic variability, but it’s important to remember that in any outdoor environment, that variability can result in some seasons being better than others. “This is an abnormal season and shouldn’t be considered in isolation as a reflection of what future seasons will look like.” He said skiing, snowboarding and snow play had still been available in NSW, Victoria and the ACT “since the June long weekend, with all resorts across Australia operating through the July school holidays and beyond”. “What this season has shown is the importance and value of the investment resorts have made in snow making, with underlying demand for snow holidays remaining strong through July and August.” Explore more on these topics Australia weather Snow Climate crisis El Niño southern oscillation news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Albanese’s resources minister celebrating the Beetaloo carbon bomb is a hell of a choice. Million Fraud Accounts Epaper Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Countdown to Antonio Guterres’ farewell begins By Ashok Ayers NEW DELHI/NEW YORK: The 81st UN General Assembly closed its general debate on Monday having asked a question in its own theme, “Restoring trust, managing transformation,” and answered it in the negative. Six days of speeches produced little that looked like trust. The great powers used the podium to argue over wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza, while the institution counted down the last 100 days of António Guterres. Donald Trump’s address on opening day leaned toward the midterms six weeks away. He defended the Iran war, floated annihilating the country, asked members to help isolate Tehran, and thanked the Security Council for backing his Gaza plan. He also claimed a Council resolution on Iranian shipping attacks drew more co-sponsors than any in history. It drew 136, but a June resolution on crimes against peacekeepers drew 153. Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian answered from the same rostrum. He held up a portrait of the slain Supreme Leader, vowed Iran would never bend the knee, and still said Tehran was open to diplomacy. Beijing sent no Xi Jinping. He was in Washington for a summit with Trump, and Vice President Han Zheng delivered the usual case for development and multilateralism, with no direct mention of Taiwan. Without naming the US, Han said Gulf states’ sovereignty must be respected and urged the “relevant country” to stop threatening Cuba. He also marked 55 years since the Assembly seated the People’s Republic. Sergey Lavrov, speaking for Moscow hours later, echoed the demand to lift the “siege” of Cuba. Vladimir Putin, like Xi, stayed home. Prime Minister Narendra Modi did not travel. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar carried India’s message on Saturday. He called Pakistan a “serial practitioner of terrorism,” said India would exercise its right to defend itself, and backed a two-state solution for Palestine. He also raised the safety of seafarers and argued that every nation has a right to shape its own AI ecosystem. On the sidelines he called the choice between BRICS and the UN a false one. It was a speech aimed as much at Islamabad’s podium as at the hall. Kyiv and Paris. Volodymyr Zelensky called Putin “patient zero” for the spread of war. Russian forces struck his party’s headquarters in Kyiv while he spoke, Kyiv officials said. He asked for more pressure on Moscow and proposed an energy ceasefire. Emmanuel Macron gave what was billed as his last address to the Assembly as president. His term ends on May 17, 2027. His most heartfelt passage was on Gaza, where he said the continuing aid blockage should shame everyone, “Shame on all of us.” He also pledged more air-defense interceptors for Ukraine ahead of winter and warned that the “law of the jungle” is spreading. Berlin, Rome and the eastern flank. Germany and Italy sent their foreign ministers, not their heads of government. Johann Wadephul spoke for Germany and Antonio Tajani, as deputy prime minister, for Italy. Wadephul’s address covered Russia’s war, AI, UN reform and global security. The sharper warnings came from the eastern flank. Latvia’s Edgars Rinkēvičs said before his speech that he would use it to highlight cyberattacks and sabotage. He said NATO has agreed that hybrid attacks could in principle trigger Article 5, though Latvia deliberately avoids commenting on that. Poland, Romania, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Serbia, Bulgaria and the Baltic presidents all took the rostrum, and Ukraine’s security was the common thread. From South Asia, Pakistan’s Shehbaz Sharif offered a line for the record, “war is a choice, but peace is a far better choice.” He thanked Trump for the May 2025 ceasefire with India and pressed Kashmir self-determination. He also warned that any attempt to divert Pakistan’s share of Indus waters would be treated as an act of war, and said Pakistan had brought Washington and Tehran to one room in Islamabad. The warning prompted Jaishankar’s reply the next day. Bangladesh’s Tarique Rahman, at the rostrum for the first time since taking office in February, spoke in Bangla for 21 minutes. He presented a “3-R” plan of recovery, restoration and reconstruction. He also backed Palestinian statehood and arms control. Nepal’s Balen Shah, the former rapper turned prime minister, was the surprise. He argued that Nepal emits under 0.1 percent of the world’s greenhouse gases yet pays disproportionately for climate change, and he pressed the money question directly. Countdown to Guterres’s farewell thus began. In his last high-level week, the Secretary-General framed inequality, climate and AI as one story. He called it “the story of power,” told members the 2030 development goals would be missed, and got a standing ovation. The rhetoric then moved into the Assembly’s six Main Committees: disarmament and security, economic and financial, social and humanitarian, special political and decolonization, budget, and legal. Their draft resolutions are normally negotiated from October and adopted in plenary by December. Apart from the budget, those resolutions are recommendations, not binding law. On Tuesday, the President of the Assembly convenes a high-level plenary meeting marking the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons. That meeting is a commemoration, not a special session, and it works from an existing resolution, A/RES/80/49. United Nations Guterres’s term ends on December 31, and the choice of his successor falls in the coming weeks. Seven candidates remain after Michelle Bachelet dropped out. In the Security Council’s straw poll on September 18, Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan led with nine “encourage” votes and five “discourage.” Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett followed with eight and six. Uganda’s Olara Otunnu had five “encourage” votes, and Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, Senegal’s Macky Sall, Ecuador’s María Fernanda Espinosa and her compatriot Ivonne A-Baki trailed. Sall, a former president, drew nine “discourage” votes. A-Baki drew ten and no “encourage.” The permanent five decide this race, and their ballots are still hidden. The next anonymous poll is set for September 29, with a colour-coded poll that distinguishes the P5 likely in October. The New York Times reported growing US opposition to Rodrigues Birkett over a “genocide” remark on Gaza, which she disputes. Lavrov has said the next chief must be “neutral, independent.” As for Macron, he is in no one’s field. He has not been nominated, and his term runs to May 2027, well past the appointment window. Guterres himself was a former prime minister, so ex-leaders can win. But this year’s only former head of state still in the race is Sall, and he is the weakest bet on the board. Grynspan is the frontrunner, but five discouraging votes in the Council are enough to end her run. The person chosen will inherit a budget crisis, a US that questions the UN’s purpose, and Security Council gridlock, none of which this week’s speeches eased.
